title: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 30-37 (Nag Hammadi Codex II, pages 39-40)
source: Nag Hammadi Codex II page photographs (Claremont Colleges Digital Library, Nag Hammadi Archive) + Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley (CC BY 4.0) + English by Mark M. Mattison (public domain)
description: Gospel of Thomas, sayings 30-37, in the Coptic of Nag Hammadi Codex II, pages 39-40, with each saying linked to the photograph of the papyrus page and an English translation.
introduction:
The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, introduced as the hidden sayings written down by Didymos Judas Thomas. The only complete copy is the second tractate of Nag Hammadi Codex II, a papyrus book in Coptic copied in the 4th century and found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945; it is now in the Coptic Museum, Cairo (inv. 10544). Greek fragments of the work survive in three Oxyrhynchus papyri (P. Oxy. 1, 654 and 655), which are not shown here.

This entry covers the sayings 30-37, which begin on codex page 39; the end of saying 37 is on page 40. The Coptic is given line by line; the small numbers are codex page and line (for example 33.5), so each line can be found on the photograph. Page and line breaks follow the Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition by Paul Dilley, which he made from the photographs of The Facsimile Edition of the Nag Hammadi Codices, the negatives shown here.

Photograph: Codex II page 39, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 49, CCDL nha 2884; Nag Hammadi Archive of the Institute for Antiquity and Christianity, Claremont Colleges Digital Library. Checked on the photograph: page 39 line 1 begins 'ⲙ̄ⲡⲁⲉⲓ ϫⲉⲡⲱ[ⲥ] ⲁⲧⲉⲉⲓⲛⲟϭ ⲙ̄ⲙ︤ⲛ︥︤ⲧ︥ⲣⲙ̄ⲙⲁ' and line 34 reads 'ⲛ̄ϫⲟⲡϫ︦ⲡ︦ · ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲟⲩ ⲧⲟⲧ[ⲉ] [ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄]ⲁⲛⲁⲩ' (the last line breaks off at a hole in the papyrus).
translator_notes: Coptic: Coptic SCRIPTORIUM edition (Paul C. Dilley), version 6.2.0, CC BY 4.0, shown in the manuscript's own spelling with words grouped as bound groups. Editorial signs are the edition's: square brackets mark letters lost in a gap (restored by the editor, or dots for the number of lost letters), a dot under a letter marks an uncertain reading, round brackets write out a letter abbreviated by a stroke at a line end, angle brackets mark letters added by the editor, curly brackets letters the editor removes, double square brackets letters erased by the scribe.

The small numbers in the Coptic are codex page and line (page.line) as marked in the edition. Where a word is divided between two lines on the papyrus, the edition sometimes keeps the word whole on one line, so a line can begin a few letters earlier or later on the photograph (for example 39.33-34, and the page change inside saying 13).

English: Mark M. Mattison, The Gospel of Thomas (public domain). Mattison's symbols: [ ] gap in the text, ( ) editorial insertion, / \ editorial correction of a scribal error. The saying headings are his.

translation.text: Jesus said, "What you hear with one ear, listen to with both, then proclaim from your rooftops. No one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket or in a hidden place. Rather, they put it on the stand so that everyone who comes and goes can see its light."

40.2ϩⲟⲧⲉ ⲁⲛ
translation.text:
His disciples said, "When will you appear to us? When will we see you?"

Jesus said, "When you strip naked without being ashamed, and throw your clothes on the ground and stomp on them as little children would, then [you'll] see the Son of the Living One and won't be afraid."
translation.scan_note: On page 39 lines 27-34; page 40 lines 1-2 (Codex II page 39, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 49, CCDL nha 2884; Codex II page 40, A-Series negative by Basile Psiroukis, Facsimile Edition p. 50, CCDL nha 2877).
